The video games most at risk from PlayStation’s physical switch-off
Plus, we speak to Gamescom about next week’s European show
Christopher Dring
Aug 20, 2026
Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube
In This Edition,
Impact of the physical switch-off
The risk of $1,000 game consoles (podcast only)
We speak to Gamescom!
Hello there!
Welcome back to another bumper edition of The Game Business.
This week, we return to the topic around PlayStation’s decision to stop manufacturing PlayStation discs. Rather than debate the decision, we’ve turned to our friends at Ampere to highlight the PS5 games that still sell well physically, and the countries where boxed games remain a strong distribution channel.
And then we chat about how publishers can manage the transition, with just under 18 months to go.
We also interview Gamescom about this year’s show, democracy and the European games sector. You can listen to all this on today’s Show above (featuring Ampere’s Piers Harding-Rolls and Gamescom’s Felix Falk). Or check out the key data, analysis and quotes below.
Enjoy!
Publishers need to prepare players for an all-digital future
In January 2028, PlayStation will stop manufacturing discs.
The data shows that video games is primarily a digital business today. However, it can vary by title, location and platform.
Our friends at Ampere Analysis looked at five PS5 games for us: Resident Evil: Requiem, Assassin’s Creed Shadows, Astro Bot, Black Myth: Wukong and Helldivers 2. It analysed what percentage of sales were made via physical retail, and broke that down by territory.
This data covers PS5 game sales only, and is unit sales up until the end of June 2026.
Family games like Astro Bot, potentially because they’re often bought at Christmas and birthday presents, are very strong in the physical space. More story-driven action adventure games such as Assassin’s Creed and Resident Evil also have a large audience of physical buyers.
Meanwhile, more online-centric games, shooters and RPGs, such as Helldivers 2 and Black Myth: Wukong, have a much smaller audience that choose to buy the boxed version.
Things also differ significantly by territory. The US is a very digital-centric market, but France is still heavily into physical. Countries like Australia, UK and Japan also have a strong boxed games retail industry.
Publishers like Capcom and Ubisoft, which make games with a strong cohort of physical buyers, will need to start preparing their fans for the physical switch-off.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is an ally in this objective. The fact the game doesn’t come in a disc will help with the education process with a large base of customers.
Nevertheless, game companies will still want to work with physical retail, including creating digital code-in-a-box products, to limit the risk of losing customers during this transition. There will be an expectation on Sony to help publishers with this, and the platform holder will also want to protect its own games (such as Astro Bot and Spider-Man). Therefore, we should expect PlayStation to develop best practices to take physical players through the transition to digital.
Some publishers will be able to start encouraging its fans to switch to digital now. For example, Capcom has a new Resident Evil game out next year, before the physical switch-off. We know from the data that the last Resident Evil (Requiem) had a strong audience of physical buyers, so the publisher will want to develop incentives to transition those users to digital with this next release.
Ultimately, the aim for the industry is to get into a position where all PlayStation game buyers in 2028 are willing to buy digitally, and know how to do it.
You can hear more on the subject in today’s edition of The Game Business Show .

Authentic, data-led engagement
Keywords Studios is the games industry’s end-to-end partner, with 13,000 people across 26 countries helping studios build, launch and support games at global scale. Supercharged by technology and shaped by long-term partnership, Keywords Studios connects specialist expertise around the player experience.
For Marketing and Player Engagement, that means helping studios understand players more clearly and build stronger relationships. From player support, trust and safety to community insight and engagement strategy, Keywords Studios helps teams respond to player needs with more relevance, care and impact.
Gamescom could sell more physical tickets, but doesn’t want to
Gamescom returns to Cologne next week, and the event is sold out of exhibitor space for the first time.
The firm is now looking to expand its space for 2027, but organizer Felix Falk says it isn’t expecting to increase the number of people coming into the show.
“We don’t want to fit too many people,” he told us. “Gamescom is not only about people on site. Last year we had 357,000 [footfall]. It doesn’t really matter if it’s 10,000 more or less, because most of the growth has been in the digital reach. We have massive reach in people tuning in from everywhere in the world, which is millions of people. That’s more important than people on site.
“Of course, we always try to find the good balance between as many people as possible, but not limiting the quality of stay. In 2019, we had a situation where we had too many people. The complaints were going up, and people were saying it was too full and too busy, and it starts to feel squeeze. So, we went down from there, and we give less tickets into the market. We could give more, we have two days already sold out, but it’s important for us that the day is perfect for everybody who is there, and it gets multiplied into the world by digital.”
Gamescom doubles down on democracy ahead of German president visit
German president Frank-Walter Steinmeier is heading to Gamescom next Thursday, as the trade and consumer show makes democracy a core theme for the 2026 event.
The event will promote democratic engagement via various events, fundraising activities, and the Gamescom Congress, which will feature discussions on the topic.
“For the first time, the highest represented of Germany, the president, is attending Gamescom,” Gamescom’s Felix Falk told The Game Business.
“That’s on the Gamescom Thursday, where we talk about the potential for games for democracy. In broader society and general media, there is a misunderstanding around games. You may remember how often there are articles about toxic behaviour in games, with a very narrow view on this community. We want to tell people that it’s especially gamers and the gaming industry who have a great potential for things like democracy.
“In our times right now, such as with all the problems GDC has, it’s so important to show where we are standing, and why diversity, and democracy, is so important for a successful game industry. And how we and our community can help with that democracy, because what studies have shown is that activism and engagement of the community is much higher than the rest of society. Gamers are more willing to donate, to collect donations, to sign petitions, to demonstrate, and to engage for things like democracy.”
Check out more from our interview with Felix in this week’s edition of The Game Business Show.
Meanwhile…
Human: Fall Flat development leaders Sitara Shefta and Will Dudley have formed a new studio called Pretty Cool Games. The UK-based, fully remote studio received start-up money from Chinese developer Hypergryph, which is best known for the RPG Arknights: Endfield.
As revealed yesterday, Arkane Studios leaders Harvey Smith, Ben Horne and Ricardo Bare have formed Black Pony Immersive. It is working on a single-player immersive sim game.
Deus Ex, Thief and Epic Mickey creator Warren Spector has announced his retirement after over forty years in game development.
The US Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism is investigating Roblox, accusing the platform of prioritizing ‘revenue and engagement’ over child safety. Roblox denies this.
Netflix is closing Night School Studio, alongside Helsinki-based Moonloot Games. Night School made recent horror hit Unhinged.
2K Games has launched Small Axe Studios. The new developer is led by EA Sports veterans and is based in the same city: Vancouver, Canada. The team is building the ‘next blockbuster sports franchise’ and wants to ‘redefine the future of sports video games’.
Nexon saw Q2 revenue rise 2% to $761 million, driven by continued success for Arc Raiders and MapleStory. Arc Raiders now has hit 16.3 million sales after selling a further 800,000 units during the quarter.
Mattel has announced the formation of Mattel Game Studios, a global development organisation that will create games based on the company’s IP. It follows the acquisition of Mattel163 in February, which was previously a joint venture with NetEase. The new group will oversee existing mobile games, and upcoming titles coming to Roblox and Fortnite.
Pokémon spin-off Pokopia has now sold five million copies worldwide.
CD Projekt has made some cuts to its Project Sirius team, which is the new multiplayer spin-off to The Witcher series. Nine employees have been cut, with a further nine to be offered roles elsewhere. The cuts were to ‘reflect the project’s needs at this stage of development’.
That’s it for today’s edition of The Game Business. Next week, we have our big CEO interview with Unity, so join us for that. Until then, thank you for reading.

title: 2026年短剧应用市场洞察
text:
短剧应用以移动端为核心，通过系列化视频故事满足用户碎片化观看及持续追剧的需求。其内容通常聚焦爱情、复仇、奇幻、家庭冲突和身份逆转等强情绪题材，并通过短小精悍的单集和悬念式叙事吸引用户持续观看。
2026 年第一季度，共有 6 款短剧应用进入全球应用下载量排行榜前 40 名，其中 FreeReels 位列第 8。短剧应用与头部社交、AI、游戏、购物及 OTT 平台同列榜单，表明短剧已从小众娱乐形式发展为全球主流应用类别。
对于发行商、广告主和媒体公司而言，短剧正成为日益值得关注的赛道。它兼具移动应用的规模优势、系列化娱乐内容带来的高用户黏性，以及应用内购和广告两方面不断扩大的变现机会。
短剧应用正在如何重塑全球移动娱乐格局？哪些市场、应用、用户互动趋势和变现策略正推动该赛道进入下一增长阶段？下载完整版《2026年短剧应用市场洞察》报告，获取深入分析。

全球短剧应用下载量持续激增，为收入增长打开空间
2026 年第一季度，全球短剧应用下载量延续快速增长态势，突破 8.5 亿次 ，同比增长 140% 。这一持续增长反映出短剧应用的全球覆盖面不断扩大，并在成熟市场及移动优先的增长型市场持续吸引用户。
应用内购（IAP）收入也继续增长，2026 年第一季度达到约 7.5 亿美元 ，同比增长 20% 。短剧应用的变现表现依然强劲，但随着成熟市场逐渐进入稳定期，增速已开始放缓。下一阶段的增长机会将转向东南亚、拉丁美洲和印度等规模庞大且增长迅速的市场。这些市场不断扩大的用户基础，有望逐步推动更深层次的用户互动和更高价值的消费。
移动优先的新兴市场推动短剧应用下载量超越 OTT 流媒体
2026 年第一季度，短剧应用下载量增长主要集中在东南亚、拉丁美洲和印度，三大市场合计贡献了全球四分之三以上的下载量。其中，东南亚以 32% 的份额位居首位，拉丁美洲和印度分别占 23% 和 22% ，且三个市场的下载量均实现三位数同比增长。
在用户获取方面，短剧应用在这些市场超越传统 OTT 流媒体的趋势也最为明显。2025 年至 2026 年第一季度，东南亚、拉丁美洲和印度的短剧应用下载量大幅攀升，表明移动原生、短小精悍的叙事形式正成为推动娱乐应用普及的重要力量。
FreeReels 领跑全球下载榜，新锐应用加速用户获取
2026 年第一季度， FreeReels 以超过 1 亿次下载量 成为全球下载量最高的短剧应用，环比增长 123% 。 NetShort 同样增长势头强劲，下载量环比跃升 196% ，位列全球第 3； Melolo 则继续在印度尼西亚、泰国和菲律宾扩大用户规模。
下载量增长榜显示，增长动能正转向较新且快速扩张的应用。 FreeReels 和 NetShort 已开始与 DramaBox 等成熟应用正面竞争； HotMiniDrama 、 LuckyDrama 、 BonusTV 和 iDrama 等新晋应用的崛起，则反映出用户获取格局正在快速变化，市场竞争日趋激烈。
DramaBox 和 ReelShort 领跑全球收入榜，NetShort 等新锐应用加剧市场竞争
2026 年第一季度， DramaBox 和 ReelShort 继续位居全球短剧应用收入榜首，两款应用的应用内购收入均接近 1.4 亿美元 。 NetShort 在头部阵营中的地位也进一步提升，同比增长 10% ，与 DramaWave 和 GoodShort 等成熟应用的差距持续缩小。
除头部应用外，收入增长动能正逐渐向新兴及腰部应用扩散。 My Drama 、 Shortical 、 Vigloo 、 AnyReel 和 Hongguo 均实现强劲收入增长，表明新平台正依托规模较小但快速扩张的收入基础加速变现，短剧市场竞争日趋激烈。
短剧正成为日常观看习惯，与 OTT 流媒体的差距不断缩小
过去一年，短剧应用的用户互动显著提升，用户总使用时长达到一年前的近 6 倍 。这表明短剧市场的增长已不再仅由下载量驱动，规模化的持续观看习惯也正在形成。
截至 2026 年 4 月，全球短剧应用日均使用时长达到 25 分钟 ，较 2025 年 1 月增长 85% ；OTT 流媒体则基本持平，维持在约 35 分钟 。东南亚引领这一转变，短剧应用日均使用时长已接近 40 分钟 ，达到与 OTT 流媒体相近的水平；印度也继续保持强劲上升势头。
头部应用加速拓展核心市场，短剧赛道竞争日趋激烈
随着头部应用围绕不同重点市场和变现模式加速扩张，短剧市场竞争日益激烈。 FreeReels 在印度和东南亚实现下载量快速增长； ReelShort 继续领跑美国市场的收入和用户互动； NetShort 正在日本、韩国和东南亚崛起，成为应用内购领域的强劲挑战者； Melolo 则依托广告变现模式，在印度尼西亚建立了庞大的受众基础。
这些应用的增长日益受到多种策略共同推动，包括付费获客、本地化广告创意、针对不同市场的内容策略，以及覆盖网站、搜索和视频平台的多元内容发现渠道。随着受众规模扩大，短剧应用也正从应用内购进一步拓展至广告变现，为发行商和广告主创造新的机遇。下载完整版《2026年短剧应用市场洞察》报告，深入了解推动该赛道进入下一增长阶段的应用、市场与关键策略。
展望未来：短剧应用进入规模扩张、用户参与和变现增长的新阶段
随着短剧应用持续拓展全球市场，该赛道正从下载量爆发式增长，迈入由用户互动、商业化能力和本地化运营所定义的全新竞争阶段。东南亚、拉丁美洲和印度等主要增长型市场的下载表现依然强劲，而收入领先地位仍集中在美国等较成熟市场。
未来，能够在大规模用户获取、更高留存、本地化叙事和多元变现之间取得平衡的应用，将更具增长优势。付费获客仍是扩大规模的重要途径，但头部应用正日益通过高频内容上新、应用内活动、本地化广告创意、网站与视频内容发现漏斗，以及广告变现等方式，构建更可持续的增长模式。

title: Will Big Walk’s 1m+ sales usher in a ‘co-op only’ game era?
text:
Will Big Walk’s 1m+ sales usher in a ‘co-op only’ game era?
And why was it a hit? Also: the latest discovery news & this week on Steam...
Simon Carless
Aug 22, 2026
∙ Paid
[The GameDiscoverCo game discovery newsletter is written by ‘how people find your game’ expert & company founder Simon Carless, and is a regular look at how people discover and buy video games in the 2020s.]
Welcome to the end of week, a good time to look into House House & Panic’s Big Walk . We ask a perhaps obvious (perhaps not?) question - why aren’t more PC/console games launching as ‘online co-op only’ in this very co-op friendly post-COVID world?
Before we start, our buddies at the Video Game History Foundation just acquired a relatively forgotten ‘90s book - ‘Computer Gaming World: Why Won’t This *& ☠️#1 Game Work?’ So yep, beyond Steam review complaints, PC compatibility issues have existed for EVER. (It features a cartoon about a chilling “configuration nightmare jungle” .)
[ LOOKING FOR MORE INSIGHT? You can get a free demo of our GameDiscoverCo Pro company-wide ‘Steam deep dive’ & console data, inc. MCP by reaching out today - >110 orgs have it. Or, signing up to GDCo Plus gets extra newsletter and Discord access, plus more.]
Game discovery news: click on that dirt, click it….
Let’s take a look at the latest game discovery & platform news, which goes a tiny bit like this:
Our look at GDCo’ latest top Steam demos for unreleased games reveals staying power for roguelike autobattler Guildrun (#1) and co-op bomb defusal game Bombanana! (#2) , but rising stars including incremental automation game Dirt Clicker (#3) & nice-looking loot-driven isometric bullet heaven-er Hellforged (#7).
Some new Bain & Co surveying of 5,000+ players , as interpreted by GI.biz , reveals: “two-thirds of players prefer familiar games or sequels, and only one in five seek new titles.” Also notable: 32% of 13-17 year olds “prefer open standbox/UGC” style content, vs. 19% for 40-49 year olds.
An unfortunate leak in the ARM Steam client revealed the official Steam Frame VR/AR headset unboxing & setup videos a little ahead of time. The main takeaway so far? Valve’s how-to videos are witty, the hardware’s design looks slick, and we’re expecting pricing & availability news VERY soon. (Next week?)
PlayStation kicking off ‘shovelware’ publishers got controversial in targeting Ternox Games & STONKS-9800 , since the stock market sim has sold decently on Steam: “Sony unilaterally terminated my PlayStation developer and publisher agreement without giving me any reason.” (Ternox previously put out ‘easy Platinum’ -ish games , tho, but Stonks is legit/decent . But.. it’s Sony’s platform to clean up!)
HowToMarketAGame has been looking at the rise of third-party Steam sales/festivals , revealing a top chart for ‘games that got in the most Festivals’ - headed by The Wandering Village (59!), Tavern Talk (55), and Dorfromantik (47). (Chris also spotted that “Cozy and Narrative… are over represented in festivals.” )
Circana has released July 2026’s U.S. game hardware (& select software*) charts , with spend down 10% YoY to $4.5b, with all sectors (software & hardware) down, and CoD: Black Ops II #1 in PC/console games. One interesting side stat : 63% of new physical games in 2026 were Nintendo, 32% PlayStation, & 4% Xbox. (*Minor intrigue: did Xbox pull its first-party digital data from Circana & GSD ? Apparently .)
The U.S. game console hardware situ in July, per Circana, is not pretty: hardware units -39% year on year, and spending -29% to $282m, “the lowest total for a July month since 2020 ($163 million).” Overall: “ PlayStation 5 unit sales fell 6% versus July 2025… Xbox Series dropped 18%.” And Switch 2 units are -51%, but vs. Month 2 of Switch 2, so maybe less bad. (Yet with a price rise upcoming , should it be better?)
Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier is reporting on another shift away from PlayStation live service games , for Horizon Hunters Gathering, but his YouTube video on the history of ‘PS x live service’ is most essential. (We understand why companies wanted to put ‘5 x successful live service games’ into their future P&L, but…)
The latest Steamworks doc ‘diff’ showing Valve’s problem of the week? “Artwork Overrides are intended to call attention to new content & updates… [but] you should not use Artwork Overrides to copy the graphical assets from another product on Steam, including DLC.” (Who’s been putting their DLC art in their main capsule image?!)
The ‘couldn’t be more on LinkedIn’ folks at Polden have put out a 35-page ‘here’s how to make your Steam game’ slideshow , and we liked its section on ‘strategy development’, i.e. what needs the mechanics fulfil, looking at game positioning & promo concepts. (A lot of people finalize the game concept & then do this.)
Microlinks: the latest Footprints ‘trad media’ charts show GTA 6 (footage leaks) & Phantom Blade Zero as most-mentioned; new on Xbox Game Pass are titles including Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy; Apple’s EU App Store rates are now set (and marginally lower) but Epic ain’t impressed , since DTC $ is disadvantaged.
Will Big Walk’s 1m usher in a co-op only game era?
It may not have escaped your notice that “cooperative multiplayer adventure about teamwork and talking” Big Walk ($20, $15 on launch discount), which launched on August 4th, has done rather well. It peaked at 46,000 Steam CCU and Panic confirmed 1 million copies sold multi-platform in ~6 days*.
(*GDCo currently estimates ~3.5m players LTD across Steam, PlayStation and Switch, and rising, with ~2m of those being PS+ subscribers thanks to a relatively rare PlayStation Plus ‘Monthly’ sub inclusion at launch.)
Anyhow, there’s a number of interesting things about Big Walk. Specifically:
It’s a more sophisticated, ‘linear journey’ take on much of the ‘friendslop’ genre, but started dev in ~2020 , way before friendslop was even a thing.
It’s from the devs of megahit Untitled Goose Game (>12m players, per GDCo) but there’s only 6% overlap in Steam players between UGG and Big Walk (!)
It had basically zero pre-release demos or betas, yet still managed to get to almost 1 million Steam wishlists at launch.
So what’s going on here, besides it being a great game? Well, we have some ideas on what Big Walk represents, trend-wise. But before we get there, let’s check some data, starting with GDCo Pro’s (auto-annotated!) estimates of the game’s wishlist journey:
So yes, the original reveal trailer at The Game Awards in December 2023 did a lot of heavy lifting, boosting the game over 100k wishlists quickly. If you look at that trailer, you’ll see the game’s premise encapsulated - a realistic-ish environment, stylized lead characters, and a promise of landscapes, mystery & puzzles to explore together .
From there, the longer gameplay trailer at Day Of The Devs during SGF 2025 sparked a lot more regular interest, and the ‘home stretch’ til release even more so. We actually think that the Myst (or more recently, The Witness )-ish vibes on the game really helped the unconventional hook of ‘there’s secrets here, but you have to play to find ‘em’.
Having said that, there’s no doubt that a lot of people playing Big Walk are coming across from traditional co-op ‘friendslop’ titles. Here’s GDCo data on games with high player overlap, who are also >8x as likely to have played than the average Steam player:
So, seeing obvious titles like PEAK (75% player overlap), Lethal Company (67%), and Meccha Chameleon (48%), you get the idea. But there’s also Tabletop Simulator at 49%, and Golf With Your Friends at 39%, an indication of a softer set of comps, distinct from the more action-y Risk Of Rain 2 (53%) and Helldivers 2 (51%).
The general view here is clear - these are games that you generally play with people that you know, likely with voice chat, as part of your regular social life . And I feel like this comes through even clearer in GDCo’s review sentiment overview:
The amount of time that ‘friends’ comes up in the positive review sentiment word cloud is unreal. And House House themselves, in this Reddit AmA , make it clear it was COVID-era virtual friend hangs that partly inspired the game:
“RE inspiration - when we started work on Big Walk we were in COVID lockdowns, and playing games together regularly with some friends who lived overseas. Big ones were things like Raft , or the ' We Were Here series ', as well as a bunch of Roblox games: Somewhere Wales , or Everest Pipkin's Dream Diary .”
Finding this quote delighted me, because I’d already intended to link at least one of these games to our conclusion. Which is: I don’t understand why more dev teams haven’t been exploring ‘co-op only’ experiences . The precedent is there:
Hazelight Studios has made a career over exclusively co-op titles and has sold tens of millions of units: A Way Out, It Takes Two, and Split Fiction.
The curiously under-the-radar We Were Here series , which we’ve profiled before for GDCo , is also a multi-million seller, blending co-op only puzzle & exploration.
Even the micro-indie horror series Fears To Fathom made a co-op only iteration, Fears To Fathom: Scratch Creek which has been doing great on Twitch and has sold ~300k copies, according to GDCo estimates.
I’m not just cherrypicking these titles - there aren’t many of them. I think devs just haven’t seen it a genre, or have fallen back to ‘co-optional’ titles with more aggressive gameplay loops. (The space may be ‘underdesigned’ for some oldskool purists?)
But it 1000% works. So the salient points are: these type of more co-op games are often super streamable (because of the voice interactions between the participants!), and if they require lower amounts of manual dexterity, they’re very accessible . And most of all, this space - ‘next game to play w/your friends’ - is a very active buyer market.
Big Walk is a special work of art - watch the Jacksepticeye YouTube video (beyond the first 5 minutes!) for the sense of wonder, open spaces and discovery it engenders . And what it says to me is: beyond more hasty (but still often v.fun) friendslop, there’s a deeper ‘co-op only’ subgenre here to explore. Players are waiting for it?
This week on Steam: Mortal Shell II, How to Fish…

title: Sensor Tower reveals the hidden impact of D2C revenue in mobile games
text:
Sensor Tower shared a glimpse of the hidden impact of direct-to-consumer revenue in mobile gaming.

Speaking at the State of Gaming Summit 2026, Sensor Tower SVP for gaming and entertainment Chirag Ambwani revealed how some mobile games are reaching 30%+ in D2C sales.

Sensor Tower is preparing a new feature for its platform that will provide estimates and insights on web store revenue. Looking at the top five genres by web store revenue share in the US during H1 2026, casino topped the list. Of the major top 100 casino titles, about 30% of revenue now stems from outside the app stores.

RPG was a close second, while tabletop also had a large share of web store sales. Strategy and particularly puzzle had a low share of D2C sales. Casino had the highest number of web store apps in the US, surprisingly followed by puzzle, despite its lack of D2C revenue compared to IAP.

Highlighting Monopoly Go, Ambwani said that while it has looked like Monopoly Go revenue is on the decline from App Store and Google Play estimates, web store sales are said to have grown substantially to around a third of its revenue.

In terms of how web stores generate their traffic, direct (users who reach a site by typing in the URL, using a bookmark or clicking a saved link) and social are the primary channels worldwide.

For Supercell, 56% of web store traffic was estimated to be driven directly, while social accounted for 37%. The Clash Royale and Brawl Stars developer works closely with its creator community on its titles, with teams dedicated to supporting these efforts.

Monopoly Go, Call of Duty: Mobile and Zynga Poker saw the vast majority of traffic driven through direct channels.

Raid: Shadow Legends saw 47% driven directly, while 49% was actually driven by social. Ambwani noted how Plarium is using Facebook and TikTok social campaigns to drive its web stores.

Sensor Tower did not give a headline figure for how much the D2C space is currently worth. In H1 2026, IAP revenue stood at around $40bn, marking a 2% decline year-over-year. It’s been around the same level for the last three years in a row. These estimates only include store revenue and not D2C, however.

Previously, an Appcharge report estimated that the D2C market could be worth as much as $17 billion or more. We’ve been tracking how much public games companies are making from their D2C strategies over recent quarters, with some companies generating around 40% or more off-store.

Video game consoles will bounce back – Here’s The Dring
Plus, the racing game Amazon abandoned has a new home
Christopher Dring
Aug 25, 2026
∙ Paid
Hello! Happy Monday. Are you heading to Gamescom? If so, maybe I’ll see you there. Although looking at my schedule, maybe not!
This week, we had the big GTA leak, and a couple of new studios opened. But the stories I’ve picked to dive into are around the worrying numbers around video game consoles.
Plus, a brand-new story (with some exclusive quotes) about Clutch, the Maverick Games racer that Amazon dropped earlier this year.
Enjoy!
‘Here’s The Dring’ is our subscriber-only edition of The Game Business. If you’d like to support us, we currently have a 75% off Summer Sale running. Not only do you receive this weekly newsletter and podcast, but we also produce a monthly market report and offer access to our events at no additional cost. Best of all? It also helps fund our main free Shows and newsletters on Tuesday and Thursday.
Consoles suffer their worst month of US sales in six years
In Brief: US console hardware revenue fell to a low not seen since July 2020, when PS4, Xbox One and Switch were in short supply due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Higher console prices, driven by the rising cost of RAM and storage, has ‘significantly’ impacted the selling rates of PS5 and Xbox Series S and X, says data firm Circana.
What You Need To Know:
July US sales of games, hardware and accessories fell 10% to $4.5 billion compared to the year before, reports Circana.
Mobile was the biggest reason for the decline, with console and PC content also dropping year-on-year.
Nintendo Switch 2 will receive a $50 price rise in September, potentially making the situation for console sales worst.
Data firm Ampere Analysis conducted a scenario analysis around what might happen if PlayStation 6 or Xbox’s Project Helix were to launch at $1,000. Assuming the new consoles are incrementally improved over the previous generation, the combined number of PS6 and Helix consoles sold after the first five years could be up to 38% lower than the combined sales of PS5 and Xbox Series S and X during the same period.
However, that isn’t a 38% total drop in console users, because there will be an increased number of players sticking with the previous generation.
Here’s The Dring:
The cinema has made quite the comeback (bear with me, this does relate to the topic).
2026 is set to be the biggest year for theatrical movies since before the pandemic. There are already five films that have exceeded $1 billion in Box Office revenue.
But… hadn’t we all decided that Netflix and the streaming wars had killed the big screen? What’s caused the resurgence?
The answer is incredibly boring… there were some popular films out. Inventive horror films, an ambitious sci-fi movie, a gothic romance and an adaptation of an epic poem. Interesting movies, ambitious movies, big franchise films and entirely new concepts. Stuff for kids, stuff for adults and everyone in-between.
It turns out for all the deep analysis of Gen Z viewing habits, the way to get people back to the cinema was to give people a reason to go back to the cinema.

Unity CEO: “The cost of building a game is coming down markedly”
CEO Matthew Bromberg gets optimistic about the future of video games
Christopher Dring
Aug 25, 2026
Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube
In This Edition,
Unity CEO Matthew Bromberg on…
Falling development costs
His positive outlook for the business
The AI ‘threat’
Plus, East vs West, the console sector, Epic Games and more
Last month, Unity CEO Matthew Bromberg took to the stage at the firm’s Unite conference in Seoul.
I watched his speech ahead of our interview, and I was struck by how positive it was. In the midst of studio closures, lay-offs, price rises and frustrated players, it was a refreshing listen.
“There is no question there’s been a tremendous amount of dislocation in our business and a lot of studios are retrenching,” Bromberg tells me. “It’s important to recognize that. We’re clearly in this moment of transition that is causing some pain.
“But I am absolutely 100% optimistic about the future. Having been doing this for some time, I’ve never spent a year in this business where people aren’t prone to doom and gloom. But the demand is not going anywhere. Human beings love interactive entertainment, and they love playing, and there is no evidence that there is some degradation in that desire.”
Matthew Bromberg at Unite Seoul
Beyond the simple fact that ‘people like games’, Bromberg is seeing a shift in how they’re being made.
“Although there’s all this disruption, the cost of building a game is coming down markedly. And that will continue. In my mind, there has never been a better time for independents to get together and make something extraordinary. I said that in Seoul. It used to be that the amount of resource you had to pour into something was the single biggest driver of whether or not you can be successful. Not that there weren’t lots of very high-profile flame outs, but the barrier was, ‘can I get 100, 200, 300 people together to do something? And can I pay for that for five years?’ That world is on the verge of changing radically.
“As a consequence, for those who are able to use the tools to take the power back in a way that creates opportunity for themselves and creates great art and entertainment for others, those folks are in a really great spot.”
Bromberg says that new platforms, like Netflix and Switch 2, are emerging. The platform economics on mobile are improving. And better games are on the way.
“The last few years was a period of optimization around known models and gameplay modalities, and that created a kind of sameness and sequelization, both literally and metaphorically,” he continues. “And it led to a disconnect between a lot of the major games that came out and how players received them. There was a lot of failure in that disconnect. But it’s hard to make hit games. It always has been and always will be. We will make great games, we’ll make them on new platforms, more people will make them than before, and everything will be fine.”
In today’s bumper edition of The Game Business Show , we chat to Bromberg about Unity’s turnaround, his approach to leadership, the AI ‘threat’, in-game ads, the future of consoles, Netflix, Unity’s friendship with Epic, the rise of China and Korea, and a whole lot more.
I’ve selected some of my favourite bits below. Alternatively, catch the entire chat via the links above.
Sponsor Message
Game-led creative production
Keywords Studios is the games industry’s end-to-end partner, with 13,000 people across 26 countries helping studios build, launch and support games at global scale. Supercharged by technology and shaped by long-term partnership, Keywords Studios connects specialist expertise around the player experience.
For global campaigns, that means creative production built around games and the audiences who play them. From trailers and key art to virtual production, campaign content and launch assets, Keywords Studios helps studios create content that understands the game, respects the audience and drives meaningful player connection.
The secret to turning around a business? Don’t be afraid
Three years ago, Unity was in trouble, not just from a business stand-point but also in the eyes of its clients who had lost trust in the firm following its controversial runtime fee plans (which it later cancelled).
Bromberg joined in 2024, and things have improved significantly since. In fact, it just delivered its best ever financial quarter.
The Unity CEO has been involved in these moments before. He helped turnaround Zynga, and at EA he rescued the MMO Star Wars: The Old Republic.
So, what’s his secret?
“It’s a really good environment to not be afraid in.”
“The most important thing is to be honest and fearless about what’s going wrong, what it is that people are unhappy about, and to authentically try to fix the problem,” he begins.
“No matter how difficult, no matter how painful, no matter how much change you have to make, no matter how much risk you need to take on, you have to commit to making it better.
“One issue that folks run into with these things is fear. They think, ‘Well, if I make all these changes, I might make it worse. The key to this whole thing is prioritization. We understand what people need and we’re going to deliver those things… but that means we’re not going to deliver a whole host of other things. And what if those things that I don’t deliver create a problem?’ Or, ‘if I’m going to make everything different, I’m probably going to have to change a lot of the people, and a lot of the ways we’re working, because it hasn’t produced the results. There’s going to be a tremendous amount of confrontation, awkwardness and pain in reformulating teams and changing executives.’
“You have to care more about the end result than you do about the daily pain. In my experience, usually folks know what the issues are to one degree or another, but they’re afraid to confront them because of what they imagine they’re going to have to do if that perception is correct. So, they pull back from understanding almost subconsciously.”
I observed there are probably a lot of companies that might benefit from that perspective.
“It’s a really good environment to not be afraid in,” he admits.
Western game developers can fight back with shorter dev cycles
Bromberg helped save The Old Republic at EA
At Unite Seoul, Bromberg highlighted the “extraordinary” rise in the number of hit games coming out of Korea and China. Certainly, the game business in those territories are in a better shape than in the US and parts of Europe.
But Bromberg is confident Western teams will battle back.
“Where the Western studios got into trouble is the development cycles, as they got elongated, that potential for dislocation with the player grows with each advancing day,” he tells us.
“When I first got to EA, I came in to run Star Wars: The Old Republic, which was an MMO that had gone very badly awry. It was a six-year development cycle, and in the six years lots of things changed, including subscription MMOs no longer being desired. It was free-to-play at that time. We had to reimagine everything fundamentally.
“What all game teams need to do is compress development cycles as much as possible, connect to players as early as possible, and build in conjunction with that player, and do that in an organic way so that when it releases, it feels connected to that community.
“The counterfactual which is, I go into a room for five years, I build this thing, and then ‘ta-da’. I made a cinematic and I expect a hit… that’s over. It’s just not going to happen anymore except for maybe a very tiny number of very highly anticipated titles. There needs to be a little bit of a rethink, and it’s happening.”
AI is not about to kill the video game industry
Earlier this year Google revealed Project Genie, which seemingly allowed people to make a video game with prompts. Multiple public game companies saw their share price fall sharply. Unity was one of those.
“Great games are still extraordinarily difficult to make,” Bromberg says. “This obsession around one-shotting games… if I had a dollar for every time I went on X, and somebody said, ‘I one-shotted this with 3DGS. The games business is over.’ People love to do that, and there’s nothing in the world I find more aggravating. And these are people who probably play lots of great games who know that it’s much more than that.”
“If I had a dollar for every time I went on X, and somebody said, ‘I one-shotted this with 3DGS. The games business is over.’ There’s nothing I find more aggravating.”
So, was he surprised how the markets reacted to Project Genie?
“It’s important to understand how the markets function now. It’s another artifact of how the world functions. Folks respond to memes. [I once told investors]: ‘My advice to you would be to not buy and sell shares based on LinkedIn posts.’ But of course, nobody cares what I think. They’re going to keep doing that. That’s the world we live in.
“And in fairness, creating a video game is a complex thing, and there aren’t a ton of people who understand what that process is like and what it requires, and how extraordinarily difficult it is. So, the fact that folks would react like that… at some level didn’t surprise me.
“But honestly, you don’t pay attention, up or down. When I started at the company, the first talk I gave I said: ‘You will have had the experience of doing the wrong thing and having the stock go up in the past. And you may have the experience now of doing the right thing and having it go down, and that’s fine. What you have to do is ground yourself in doing the right thing. And all the rest of it takes care of itself over time’.”
Console costs will go down and new games will bring in younger players
Unity works across all platforms, including PC, console, mobile… even Netflix and Fortnite. It knows where things are growing, and where things are challenged. And one area that appears challenged right now is the console space.
“It’s been a difficult time for console hardware, which is under genuine cost pressure,” Bromberg notes. “It’s unprecedented and it’s wacky. The idea that things get more expensive is the upside down of how it usually works. But that doesn’t mean that great console entertainment isn’t going to be consumed in massive quantities, and we’ll see that with GTA.
“I think of the cost pressures as being temporary. Clearly from a demographic perspective, the console is a little bit challenged as the core consumer ages. I’m not sure that the console business is replacing older players with as many younger players as it used to. But it was not very long ago that every teenager was playing Fortnite on console, so much so that it was thought to be a problem.
“The platform is vibrant. We will get more hit console entertainment. Costs will come down. And the industry will make games that will attract younger consumers over time.”
Indeed, it all comes down to the games, concludes Bromberg.
“There will be better, more engaging games built over the next ten years than were ever built over the prior ten. We’re just beginning to scratch the surface of the level of persuasion and the intensity of engagement that we’re going to achieve. It’s crazy to think that the best years of this business are not in front of us.”
Check out our full interview with Bromberg, which dives deeper into AI, discusses Unity’s ad business, its partnership with Epic, and more.
And then join us on Thursday for our Gamescom edition of The Game Business Show. Until then, thank you for reading.

Game discovery news: hey, Wardogs, Sally Face 2..
Let’s start out by having a hack at the newest notable game platform & discovery news. And we’ve spotted the following:
Looking at GDCo Pro's estimates of 'trending' unreleased Steam games , Aug 17th-24th (above), AA 100-player FPS Wardogs (#1) is looking rather hot, given its playtest hit 105k CCU on Steam recently. And at #2, it's the newly announced Sally Face 2 , which follows up the very creepy cult hit 2D adventure.
Friendslopper Dear Passengers is at #3, the recently re-hyped Phantom Blade Zero hits #4, and there's a brand new entry at #5 for Northern wilderness co-op survival-er Rerouted . And there’s 2 other new announces: visual novel Tulpa The Unseen Lover (#7) and '00s Need For Speed-y indie street racer Heatwarped (#10).
Steam is testing personalization on normally curated Midweek Deals , which “are featured on the Steam homepage… from Monday at 10am Pacific until Thursday at 10am Pacific. There are up to six Midweek slots per week.” (If you’re logged in, you’ll see a wide selection of discounted games this week, largely different per account.)
Remember timed console exclusivity? It’s always been lurking, and Silent Hill: Townfall’s latest trailer shows a prime new example : “Alongside reiterating that Townfall is a PS5 console exclusive, a caption confirmed: ‘Also available on PC. Not available on other consoles until at least 6 months after release date’.”
As Geoff Keighley reminds us , “Valve was founded 30 years ago today [on August 24th, 1996] by Gabe Newell and Mike Harrington.” PC Gamer has more on the history , spanning Half-Life and sequels, the Source Engine, and - of course - a little PC gaming platform called Steam. (Congrats!)
This ResetEra thread on the state of ‘big box store’ physical retail for games documents the decline of Xbox footprint, w/just “a small case for [Xbox] consoles with some controllers…. Honestly even the PlayStation section has shrunk a bit… The Nintendo one is still large… and I think is the only one that still has a demo unit.”
We don’t generally see indie devs announcing an immediate 50,000 pre-orders on Epic Games Store , but that’s what ‘magical girl’ co-op action RPG Kernel Hearts managed, thanks in large part to an exclusive Fortnite skin for those who pre-ordered . (That cross-promo is, at least initially, looking quite effective…)
For those devs who have Steam pre-orders for their game, there’s a change to SteamWorks documentation explaining that (encrypted!) preload should ideally be activated for “Games with large file sizes [and] extremely anticipated games”, and warning that multiple big pre-load patches can clutter a Steam player’s hard drive.
Roblox things: some bots got blocked in Roblox , leading to CCU decreases; Offpath’s Tim Elliott spotted that “ Steal an Egg on Roblox set a record for fastest time to 500k CCU in just 497 hours of organic traffic” ; doomscrolling and short-form video features “are no longer allowed in games targeted towards children on Roblox .”
More ‘web browser gaming’ - not cloud-streamed, locally run? Exhibit #1: Entity just raised $5.8m “to bring console-quality games to what it calls the ‘new web.’” Exhibit #2: Moon Studios’ Thomas Mahler has a browser-first version of new game Luma (also w/downloadable PC/Mac versions.)
Finally: ‘keyword squatting’ is still an issue on consoles, i.e. picking a game name that includes words from another popular game’s title. The latest unfortunate example would be Lethal Corporation on Switch eShop , which clones the Lethal Company logo but isn’t even co-op. (Can’t we do more about this, platforms?)

How have hit PC genres changed since 2021?
Look, the PC game market has changed significantly over the last 5 years. But how can we quantify that? At GameDiscoverCo, we have a lot of underlying data on this, so we thought we’d use ‘purified’ versions of Steam tag clouds to compare the market in 2021 to that of 2025 .
Rather than just cloud-ifying all tags on all games released in that year, we’re a) keeping this to ‘genre’ tags , b) excluding the ‘mega-genres’ like strategy, action, and RPG c) using tags only from new games with >50k copies sold in that year , and d) only using tags that are ranked in the Top 5 for a game - i.e. the most important.
The results (above) for 2021 are interesting, and def. feel like a ‘five years ago’ market snapshot: survival is huge, as is city builder and action RPG, with JRPG, turn-based strategy & base building also big contenders. Now, let’s look at 2025, same view:
Well, that’s a difference. At first, I presumed that maybe Roguelite (#1, up 39 spots!) and Roguelike (#2, up 37 spots) might have been introduced as tags since 2021. But nope, SteamDB’s ‘tag additions by date’ say they’ve been around since ~2017, just under-used. (So yep - the ‘run-based randomness’ trend is kinda on fire.) Other things of note:
Action RPG continues to be a super-solid genre: it covers a multitude of sins, from Souls-likes to action/strategy hybrids, but it’s up one spot to #4 vs. 2021.
JRPG, RTS, and Turn-Based Strategy are on the way down: they’re down 24, 17, and 19 spots overall. Why? We suspect more hybrid-genre, roguelite-y games.
Life Sim is on the way up, City Builder slipping down : life sim, which a large # of cozy games brush up against, is up 31 spots (!) to #6. And City Builder is still in the Top 10, but is down 5 spots to #7.
Other big gainers, subgenre-wise: Idler - up 46 spots to #15, and Racing - up 22 spots to #9, mainly due to more indie/niche racers? And on the other side, Survival Horror is down 17 spots to #26, whereas Psychological Horror is down 6 to #13. (We still think horror is hot, mind you - just a particular uneasy/creepypasta flavor, maybe?)
But, I hear you yelling, is ‘units sold’ really a good comparison? There are lots of cheaper games (some of them shorter, some of them very replayable!) in 2025 vs. 2021. Well, fair, cos:
The Top 10 games by units we pulled for 2021 included only one game under $20 ( Devour, an early Phasmophobia-like) , and five at $60 (inc. Forza 4, Halo Infinite.) Even co-op breakout It Takes Two was a ‘mid-price’ hit at $40.
The Top 10 games by units for 2025 has three big hits under $10 (R.E.P.O., Peak and RV There Yet?) and only two games at $60+ ( Battlefield 6, Monster Hunter Wilds.)
That’s a bit more anecdotal, of course. (Though we’ve surveyed for decreasing price before .) But across all the games we surveyed, 2021’s 261 games had a median current USD price of $19.99, and 2025’s 469 games were 15% less at a $16.99 median.
So if you think we’re over-concentrating on cheap $5 games that sell 50k copies way more easily, let’s switch things up to be revenue-first. Here’s the same tag clouds, but with output by >$1m gross Steam revenue in that year, starting with 2021’s releases:
This tag cloud, from 196 games, looks fairly similar to the ‘units’ one for 2021, but with Survival downgraded quite a bit, and FPS and JRPG downshifted not much at all. (It’s good to know it doesn’t make a titanic difference.)
The good news: it’s our new baseline to compare to the top Steam tags for 2025 by revenue, as inexpensive games that sold 50-100k units are now excluded from this tag soup , while $50 games that sold 30k copies during that year make it in here :
This includes top tags from 311 games, 59% more than 2021.
Well, some of this is kinda the same - Roguelite is again #1 in 2025 (up 37 spots from 2021) , and Roguelike is #2 (up 28 spots from 2021!) But here’s differences we spotted:
Some key genres like FPS and JRPG drop less in this view: FPS is only down 2 spots to #3 here, and JRPG down 8 spots to #10 (vs. #28 in the ‘copies sold’ view!)
Hack And Slash is an intriguing over-performer: we think this tag gets added to a lot of more $ ARPG & Souls-likes, and even some roguelikes, and it’s up 11 to #5, vs. #12 in the ‘units’ view.
Immersive Sim makes a bit more of a bid for interest: this subgenre is making a bit of a stealth comeback, and there’s indies in the space like Shadows Of Doubt - so it’s up 13 spots to #15, higher than the ‘units-only’ version.
We find all this pretty interesting because, minus all those other less genre focused Steam tags (no disrespect, Dwarves and Capybaras ), it feels like a true ‘flavor test’ of the zeitgeist right now. (Whether we like the direction of flow or not.)
And that’s it! To write this up, I’ve been consulting a ‘cheat sheet’ documenting the exact tag ranking changes from 2021 to 2025 (thx Alejandro!) And heck, we’re going to leave it in the newsletter in its raw form below, because it’s pretty interesting. Hurray!
[A final reminder: we’re not saying you have to make games in these subgenres, or that Steam tagging is a perfect way of documenting them. We are, however, saying that this is real data on new game popularity via Steam tags, regardless of dev team size and dev time.]
